sweep_summary: Both works with stress in the title are Glottolog duplicates of the catalog's own deciding source, Remijsen's 2001 LOT 49 dissertation (Glottolog dates one copy 2002 with a dead Papuaweb URL; the other is the MPI handle copy behind a bot wall). The open LOT PDF is held by the project and was re-read: it confirms the 'lexical' coding (contrastive penult vs final stress, minimal pairs, acoustic support) and the catalog's secondary rule (contrast confined to penult-/a/ words; constraints I-III pp.106-107, 122). Additional stress-relevant works found via Crossref and the Glottolog langdoc list but not in the item list: Remijsen 2002 LabPhon 7 chapter (published version of ch. III; paywalled, medium priority) and Remijsen 2001 Language and Speech (dialectal tone variation; paywalled, low), plus van der Leeden 1983/1993 (print only; earlier four-toneme analysis that Remijsen supersedes), van der Leeden 1997 and Kawira 1986 (not found). Arnold 2018 (held by the project) is a consistent secondary summary. No change to the catalog is warranted; no new statement supersedes the current source.

new_statements.quote: I. If a polysyllabic word has a vowel other than /a/ in the penultimate syllable, it can only have penultimate stress. Alternatively, when a polysyllabic word has the vowel /a/ in the penultimate syllable, then stress is contrastive, either on the penultimate or on the final syllable. II. If a polysyllabic word has a vowel other than /a/ in the penultimate syllable, the vowels of penultimate and final syllables are usually the same. ... III. Words with penultimate stress can only have a High toneme; words with final stress can have either the High or the Rise tonemes. [pp.106-107] ... Contrastive stress, therefore, is limited to words with the penultimate syllable vowel /a/, and mostly with final vowel also being /a/ [p.122]

This is the same source the catalog already cites and the catalog's 'lexical' kind plus its secondary rule already encode exactly these passages ( correction of 2026-09-12). Nothing read in this search of works with stress in the title is more authoritative or more first-hand.

audit.reasoning: The deciding quotation is verbatim in the held Remijsen 2001 LOT dissertation at the stated pages (p.2, p.53; sub-regularities pp.105-106; secondary locators p.18, p.49 also verified). The source is the definitive fieldwork-based phonological and instrumental study of Ma'ya word prosody by the specialist on the language, superseding van der Leeden 1993; no reference grammar has been published, and the later literature (Arnold 2018, downloaded, pp.9-10) restates the same analysis: lexical tone confined to the final syllable, lexical stress contrastive between penult and final. Coding 'lexical', right edge, is exactly what the source says. works still to obtain are low-priority corroboration (refereed versions, the superseded competing analysis), none likely to change the classification.

tone.summary: Tonogenesis of Ma'ya-Matbat tone; Ma'ya H/Rise(/Fall) system as comparandum.
tone.says: Bottom-up comparison of tonal correspondences across Ambel, Ma'ya and Matbat; concluded tone was innovated in a common ancestor of Ma'ya and Matbat and separately in Ambel (per web summary and Arnold 2025 OL sec.1/sec.7, where the author revises that conclusion). Bears on the origin of the Ma'ya (incl. Wauyai) High/Rise system.

tone.says: Reanalyses van der Leeden's four-toneme system as three paradigmatically contrastive values on the final syllable of content roots - High /3/, Rise /12/ and toneless (stress only) - plus lexically contrastive stress on the penult or final syllable, independent of tone; acoustic study shows stress is cued by duration, vowel quality, spectral tilt, not by f0, while tone is cued by f0; Ma'ya + Papiamentu named as the only reported hybrid systems with contrastive stress AND lexical tone.

tone.says: Citation + Remijsen's summary (2001:47-50): descriptive phonology of Salawati Ma'ya distinguishing four tonemes - High /3/, Rising /12/, Falling /21/, Low /1/ - marked on every syllable (e.g. Ga'le12 Ma'ya3), with variable stress and a stress-shift rule and morphological tone; Remijsen calls it 'the discovery of lexical tone in Ma'ya by van der Leeden' and reanalyses it with fewer tonemes.
